analysis.one_liner: Taxes private equity and hedge fund managers' profit shares as ordinary income instead of lower capital-gains rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in the Ways and Means Committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity, hedge, and real estate partnerships often take a share of their investors' profits, known as carried interest, and pay tax on it at the lower long-term capital gains rate instead of the higher rates that apply to wages. This bill would have taxed those profits as ordinary income, made them subject to self-employment tax, repealed a 2017 law that partially shields them, and imposed a 40% penalty on underpayments from dodging the rules. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit because the tax burden shifts from everyday income earners onto a small group of high-earning fund managers; the added revenue could reduce deficits or fund public services. Workers who pay payroll taxes on their wages would also see fund managers brought under the same self-employment tax rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill recharacterizes the capital gain allocated to an 'investment services partnership interest' as ordinary income, which is taxed at rates up to 37% instead of the 15-20% long-term capital gains rate [S2].
It repeals Section 1061 of the tax code, the 2017 provision that gives fund managers a three-year holding-period break on carried interest [S2].
It makes investment services partnership income count as net earnings from self-employment, so fund managers pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on it like other workers do [S2].

It closes side doors: gains shifted into disqualified interests or other investment entities tied to management services are also taxed as ordinary income, and tax avoidance triggers an elevated 40% accuracy penalty [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate investment partnerships, who would pay tens of thousands of dollars more per dollar of carried interest; the partnerships themselves face new valuation, reporting, and recordkeeping requirements.

drawbacks.text: Defenders of carried interest argue it is a genuine return on managers' own invested capital and risk-taking, and that taxing it as ordinary income would discourage long-term investment in companies, real estate, and infrastructure [S2].
The bill's anti-abuse rules, valuation rules, and tiered-partnership rules would impose significant compliance costs on partnerships and require the Treasury to write many new regulations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes to a broad, diffuse public (more tax collected from a very small, very high-earning group), while the cost falls on roughly the wealthiest sliver of earners, most of whom can afford it. The main honest objection is the complexity of policing the boundary between managers' compensation and genuine capital returns, which the bill addresses with detailed carve-outs for real capital contributions and family partnerships, but which would inevitably invite litigation and planning.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2024, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and the committee never held a hearing or markup before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on October 11, 2024 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law [S4].
No other action was ever taken: the bill received no cosponsors [S3], the committee never scheduled a markup or hearing [S4], and no floor vote ever occurred [S4].

The bill was named for Rep. Bill Pascrell, a New Jersey Democrat who had long pushed to end the carried interest break and died in August 2024; this is widely reported, not shown in the congressional record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fund managers who receive carried interest are better off, because they keep the lower capital-gains tax rate and the exemption from self-employment tax on that income. No committee action was ever taken, so the tax structure they benefit from remained untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers, who kept the tax break

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax carried interest as ordinary income

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of potential support was never tested.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: The bill taxes their carried interest at ordinary income rates, subjects it to self-employment tax, and applies a 40% penalty to avoidance schemes, directly cutting their after-tax income. Their interest in keeping the current tax treatment runs against the general taxpayer's interest in an even tax base.

industries.industry: Venture capital and real estate investment partnerships
industries.note: Real estate partnerships and REIT-held partnerships fall within the bill's definition of investment partnerships, though with some carve-outs, so their managers would pay more tax on profit shares. Ordinary taxpayers would bear less of the tax burden as a result.
The bill requires new reporting, recordkeeping, and valuation of partnership interests, creating compliance work. This is a minor effect on consumers.
